relations.note: Ascanius is normally Aeneas's son by Creusa and his dynastic heir.
Ascanius governs the Trojan camp while Aeneas is absent.

relations.myth: Escape from Troy and migration to Italy
relations.note: Aeneas leads Ascanius from Troy and takes him through the Mediterranean migration.
Aeneas views Cloelia’s future deed represented on his divine shield.
She conducts Aeneas safely through the underworld and brings him to Anchises.
The Sibyl instructs and guides Aeneas through the underworld.
The Sibyl foretells Aeneas’ Italian wars and instructs him about burial and the golden bough.
Evander hosts Aeneas and supplies troops under Pallas.
Evander welcomes Aeneas, tours future Rome, and directs him toward Etruscan aid.
Evander entrusts his son Pallas and an Arcadian cavalry force to Aeneas.
Cocles appears as a future Roman exemplar on Aeneas’ divine shield.
Aeneas marries Latinus's daughter and establishes his Italian dynasty.
Lavinia is given in marriage to Aeneas after his arrival in Italy.
Aeneas founds Lavinium and names the city after Lavinia.
Aeneas awards Euryalus victory prizes and gives Nisus a consolation shield.
Nisus serves among Aeneas's Trojan followers and dies during a night raid.

relations.myth: Trojan service and mission through the Rutulian lines
relations.note: They follow Aeneas and volunteer to carry news to him.
Pallas fights as Aeneas's young ally under his protection.
Pallas welcomes Aeneas, becomes his allied commander, and fights beside the Trojans.
Aeneas prepares Pallas’s funeral procession and later kills Turnus in his name.
Evander places Pallas under Aeneas as his teacher in warfare.
Canonical Roman genealogy makes Romulus Aeneas's remote descendant through the Alban kings.
Compressed Greek genealogical variants make Romulus or Romus Aeneas's son.

relations.myth: Rivalry for Lavinia and Latin sovereignty
relations.note: Turnus and Aeneas rival one another for Lavinia and political supremacy.
Turnus wages war against Aeneas as rival claimant to Lavinia.
Turnus commands the Italian coalition against Aeneas and repeatedly seeks battle with him.
Aeneas kills the defeated Turnus after recognizing Pallas's belt.
Livy reports a version making Ascanius the Italian-born son of Lavinia.
Ascanius leaves prosperous Lavinium to Lavinia, described as his mother or stepmother.

relations.myth: Nisus and Euryalus undertake the night mission
relations.note: Ascanius promises Euryalus wealth, status, and care for his mother before the fatal mission.
Ascanius gives Euryalus his sword and promises rewards and maternal protection.

relations.myth: Nisus and Euryalus undertake the night mission
relations.note: Nisus requests Ascanius’s permission, receives instructions, and carries messages toward Aeneas.

relations.myth: Mission from the besieged Trojan camp
relations.note: They present their mission to Ascanius and undertake to reach Aeneas.
Romulus descends remotely from Ascanius through the Alban royal succession.
Ascanius governs the camp besieged by Turnus, though they never duel directly.
Corneille makes Camille the lover of the Alban Curiace.
Horace kills Camille after she denounces Rome and mourns Curiace.
Corneille names Horace's sister Camille, replacing the ancient unnamed Horatia.
Tarpeia fights beside Camilla while carrying a bronze axe.
Camilla commands cavalry for Turnus and summons him to defend the city.
Virgil juxtaposes images of Cocles and Cloelia without a personal encounter.
Florus groups Cocles and Cloelia among Rome’s republican marvels.
The Polybian variant makes Pallas Evander’s grandson through Lavinia.
Pallas is Evander’s son in Virgil’s dominant tradition.
Evander sends Pallas as military protégé and companion under Aeneas.
Evander and Pallas worship Hercules together when Aeneas arrives.
Evander receives and laments his slain son’s body and demands vengeance.
Evander entrusts Pallas to Aeneas, embraces him, then laments his returned body.
One Greek genealogy makes Romos a descendant of Evander’s daughter Roma.
Competing traditions credit Evander or the twins with founding the Lupercalia.
After Turnus kills Pallas, Evander awaits vengeance through Aeneas.
They act successively as Roman saviours but never meet in ancient narrative.

relations.myth: Contest for precedence among courage exemplars
relations.note: Valerius rhetorically asks Romulus to yield precedence because Cocles preserved his city.
The Polybian genealogy names Evander’s daughter Lavinia as Pallas’s mother.

relations.myth: Parallel liberation through a woman’s death
relations.note: Verginia’s fate is explicitly presented as a second Lucretia-style liberation from tyranny.

relations.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
relations.note: Nisus kills Remus’ attendants and then decapitates Remus.

relations.myth: Night raid against the Rutulian camp
relations.note: They massacre Turnus’ sleeping troops; his army later displays their severed heads.
Pallas accepts Turnus’s challenge and grazes his shoulder with a spear.
Turnus’s spear pierces Pallas’s shield, armor, and chest, killing him.
Turnus plants his foot upon Pallas’s corpse and strips away his decorated baldric.

relations.myth: Tarpeia's attempted disarming of the Sabines
relations.note: Tarpeia secretly warns Romulus that she plans to disarm the Sabines.
Romulus holds Tatius's daughter Tarpeia under compulsion before her escape or betrayal.

god_relations.note: Aeneas is her son by the mortal Anchises.
She carries wounded Aeneas from battle until Diomedes wounds her.
Venus obtains divine armor for Aeneas before the Italian war.
Venus purifies and anoints Aeneas, completing his transformation into Indiges.
Apollo shelters Aeneas, restores him, and creates a battlefield phantom.
Apollo's oracles guide Aeneas during his Mediterranean migration.
Artemis heals the wounded Aeneas together with Leto.
Poseidon removes Aeneas from danger so the Dardanid line can survive.
Neptune calms the storm threatening Aeneas's fleet.
Aeneas descends from Zeus through Dardanus and the Assaracid line.
Zeus's providential order guarantees the survival and future rule of Aeneas's dynasty.
Jupiter repeatedly confirms and directs Aeneas's destined settlement in Italy.
Jupiter approves Venus's request that Aeneas be admitted among the gods.
Juno persecutes Aeneas because of Troy, Carthage, and Paris's judgment.
Juno accepts Aeneas's settlement if Trojan identity merges into Latin.
Aeneas witnesses signs of Minerva's wrath against Troy and the violated Palladium.
Aeneas dedicates the slain Mezentius's armor and spoils to Mars.
Mercury commands Aeneas to abandon Carthage and resume his Italian mission.
Disguised as Ascanius, Cupid inflames Dido while embracing Aeneas.
At Juno's request, Aeolus releases winds against Aeneas's fleet.
Cybele supplies sacred Trojan timber used for Aeneas's ships.
Cybele transforms Aeneas's threatened ships into sea nymphs.
After seeing the golden bough, Charon ferries the living Aeneas.
Aeneas passes Cerberus after the Sibyl drugs the monster.
Aeneas saves and transports Troy's ancestral gods during his escape.
The Penates appear in a dream and direct Aeneas toward his destined settlement.
Venus is Ascanius’s divine paternal grandmother through Aeneas.
Venus removes the sleeping Ascanius to Idalium while Cupid assumes his appearance.
The Julian genealogy traces Ascanius’s Trojan ancestry remotely to Jupiter.
Jupiter confirms the omen over Ascanius with thunder and a blazing star.
Ascanius prays to Jupiter before firing the arrow that kills Numanus.

god_relations.myth: Cupid impersonates Ascanius at Dido’s banquet
god_relations.note: Cupid assumes Ascanius’s form, gifts, and social place while the boy sleeps.

god_relations.myth: The tame stag and outbreak of war
god_relations.note: Juno indirectly endangers Ascanius by having Allecto turn his hunt into war.
Apollo praises Ascanius’s valor after he kills Numanus Remulus.
Disguised as Butes, Apollo orders Ascanius to abstain from further combat.
Mercury invokes Ascanius’s owed Italian kingdom while warning Aeneas to depart.
Modern scholarship tentatively identifies the Julian god Vediovis with a deified Iulus.
Metabus dedicates Camilla to Diana, whose devoted virgin servant she remains.
Apollo grants Arruns success in killing Camilla but denies his safe return.
Vulcan makes the shield bearing a representation of Cloelia’s escape.
Virgil names Deiphobe as the daughter of Glaucus.
Deiphobe serves as Apollo’s priestess and prophetic medium at Cumae.

god_relations.myth: Apollo possesses Deiphobe during her prophecy
god_relations.note: Apollo’s possession alters her face, voice, hair, color and bodily bearing.
Apollo seeks sexual compliance, but the Sibyl refuses him.
Apollo grants her requested lifespan and conditionally offers perpetual youth.
Hecate appoints the Sibyl over the groves of Avernus.
Hecate teaches the Sibyl the punishments imposed by the gods.
The Sibyl invokes Hecate before entering the underworld with Aeneas.
Under the Sibyl’s direction, Aeneas deposits Proserpina’s sacred bough at her threshold.
Venus indirectly assists the Sibyl’s mission by sending doves to guide Aeneas.
The Sibyl explains Aeneas’ lawful mission and displays the bough, persuading Charon to carry them.
The Sibyl subdues Cerberus with a soporific honey-cake and passes while he sleeps.
Hermes is Evander’s father in the divine Arcadian genealogy.
Hermes fathers Evander by an unnamed daughter of Ladon.
The Romanized genealogy names Mercury as Evander’s father.
Carmenta is Evander’s prophetic mother in the Romanized divine genealogy.
His prophetic mother accompanies, consoles, and guides him during exile.
One alternative tradition makes Carmenta Evander’s wife rather than mother.
Themis is the Greek designation of Evander’s prophetic mother.
The prophetic Themis guides Evander’s colonists in selecting their settlement.
Nicostrata is an alternative name for Evander’s prophetic maternal figure.
Faunus receives Evander’s colonists hospitably and grants them land.
Evander’s Arcadians establish her wine-free rites served by women.
Consus’s Roman festival is equated with the Arcadian equestrian rite.
Some antiquarian traditions make Apollo guide Evander’s migration.
Evander hosts Hercules and recognizes his divine parentage and future apotheosis.

god_relations.myth: Foundation of the Ara Maxima rites
god_relations.note: Evander establishes Hercules’ first Roman honors and performs sacrifice.
Evander celebrates Hercules and narrates his defeat of Cacus to Aeneas.
Vulcan forges Aeneas’ shield bearing Cocles’ future bridge defense.
Cocles’ statue is placed in Vulcan’s precinct after a lightning prodigy.
Lavinia is Faunus’ granddaughter through her father Latinus.
Curtius extends his hands downward and consecrates his life to them.
Jupiter requires Rome's greatest good, which Curtius supplies through self-sacrifice.
Nisus invokes Jupiter or any god favoring his plan; none visibly intervenes.
Nisus prays to her to guide his missiles; both throws strike.
Nisus personifies Fortune as potentially preventing Euryalus from burying him.
An incompatible Polybian genealogy makes Pallas the son of Heracles and Lavinia.
Carmenta is Pallas’s grandmother through her son Evander.
Carmenta prophetically warns her grandson about his fatal armor and coming avenger.
The Roman genealogy makes Mercury Pallas’s great-grandfather through Carmenta and Evander.
Pallas attends Pallanteum’s annual sacrifice celebrating Heracles’ defeat of Cacus.
Pallas invokes Heracles through hospitality; Heracles hears and weeps but cannot save him.
Jupiter prevents their duel because both youths are destined for greater opponents.
Jupiter tells Heracles that Pallas’s appointed day cannot be altered.

god_relations.myth: Regulus keeps his oath to Carthage
god_relations.note: Jupiter implicitly guarantees the enemy oath that compels Regulus to return.
Fortune overturns Regulus's success after his arrogant peace demands.
Seneca portrays Regulus as morally victorious over Fortune through steadfast suffering.

god_relations.myth: Herculean framing of the Bagradas serpent
god_relations.note: Silius models Regulus's serpent exploit on Herculean monster combats without identifying them.
Horace contrasts captive Romans' forgetfulness of Vesta with Regulus's fidelity.
Mars fathers Romulus and Remus with Rhea Silvia.
Mars carries Romulus to heaven or obtains his divine admission.
Jupiter’s vultures communicate divine approval during the brothers’ disputed augury.
Jupiter fulfills his promise and authorizes Romulus’ admission among the gods.
Romulus dedicates Acron’s armor and a temple to Jupiter Feretrius.
Romulus vows a temple; Jupiter Stator halts the Romans’ flight.
After disappearing, Romulus is identified with the older Roman god Quirinus.
The twins’ mother Rhea Silvia serves as Vesta’s priestess.
Faunus shares the Lupercalian cult setting later connected with the twins.

god_relations.myth: Games and abduction of the women
god_relations.note: Romulus stages Consus’ games as the occasion for abducting neighboring women.
Romulus later incorporates or honors Hercules’ preexisting cult at Rome.
Juno arranges for Hersilia to join the deified Romulus.
As a Vestal, Tarpeia fetches water and tends obligations associated with Vesta.
Tarpeia's desire and betrayal violate Vesta's sacred fire and her Vestal duties.
Tarpeia draws ritual water from a spring in Silvanus's branching house.
Tarpeia's betrayal enables the Sabines to capture Jupiter's ancient threshold.
Dedication of the hill to Jupiter causes Tarpeia's bones to be removed.

god_relations.myth: Divine opening of the Sabine gate
god_relations.note: After Tarpeia admits the Sabines, Juno unbars the gate supporting their assault.
After Tarpeia's betrayal, Venus enlists nymphs to flood the Sabines' path.
Juno supports Turnus through Allecto, Iris, Juturna, and repeated interventions against Aeneas.

god_relations.myth: Phantom Aeneas and the departing ship
god_relations.note: Juno lures Turnus aboard ship with a phantom Aeneas and carries him safely to Ardea.
Jupiter refuses to alter Turnus’s fate, ends Juno’s resistance, and sanctions the final settlement.
Venus heals Aeneas’s wound, enabling him to resume his pursuit of Turnus.
Turnus’s borrowed sword shatters when he strikes armor forged by Vulcan for Aeneas.
Turnus tries to burn Cybele’s sacred ships, but they transform into sea-nymphs.

god_relations.myth: Spear lodged in Faunus’s sacred olive
god_relations.note: Turnus prays to Faunus when Aeneas’s spear lodges in the god’s sacred wild olive.

Abaris.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Abaris.note: Euryalus kills Abaris during the night raid.

Acca.note: Camilla's closest companion receives her last words and carries them to Turnus.

Acestes.note: Acestes hosts Aeneas and receives Trojan settlers in Sicily.
Acestes is the Sicilian ally hosting the Trojan community and Ascanius’s mounted display.
Acestes is the Sicilian host and ruler associated with the games.

Achates.note: Achates is Aeneas's closest recurring companion and confidant.
Achates brings Deiphobe to Aeneas before her prophetic possession.

Acoetes.note: His aged attendant accompanies Pallas in life and follows his bier grieving.

Aethon.note: Pallas’s horse follows his bier riderless, without ornaments, and weeping.

Aletes.note: Aletes praises Nisus and Euryalus in the council presided over by Ascanius.
Aletes praises their courage and interprets it as divine favor.

Allecto.note: Allecto inflames Ascanius’s hounds and directs the unwitting hunter toward Silvia’s stag.
Allecto approaches Turnus disguised as Calybe before revealing her Fury form.
Allecto thrusts divine torches into Turnus and fills him with supernatural war-fury.

Amastrus.note: Camilla kills Amastrus, son of Hippotas.

Amata.note: Amata opposes Aeneas's marriage to Lavinia and supports Turnus.

Anchemolus.note: Pallas attacks and kills Anchemolus during his battlefield advance.

Anchises.note: Aeneas is the son of Anchises and Aphrodite.
Aeneas carries his aged father from burning Troy.
Anchises teaches Aeneas the soul-cycle and reveals future Romans.

Anchises.myth: Flame omen and escape from Troy
Anchises.note: Anchises interprets Ascanius’s flame omen and flees Troy with him.
Ascanius leads a mounted squadron during games honoring his dead grandfather.
The Sibyl delivers Aeneas to Anchises but has no recorded substantive dialogue with him.
Young Evander receives a cloak, weapons, and bridles from Anchises.
They compete in the footrace held in Anchises’ honor.

Anchurus.note: Pseudo-Plutarch pairs their parallel voluntary leaps, though they never meet.

Anna.note: Aeneas receives Dido's refugee sister in Latium.

Anna Perenna.note: Lavinia promises sisterly treatment but secretly suspects and plots against Anna.

Arcadian companions.note: Pallas commands and rallies the retreating Arcadians, who later carry his body.

Arruns.note: Arruns stalks Camilla and mortally wounds her with a spear.

Assaracus.note: Aeneas descends through Assaracus's collateral Trojan royal line.

Astyanax.note: Andromache compares Ascanius’s appearance and age to her dead son Astyanax.

Atlas.note: Evander invokes shared descent from Atlas linking Arcadian and Trojan houses.

Atys.note: Atys leads another mounted squadron alongside Ascanius in the Trojan youth display.

Augustus.myth: Horatian juxtaposition of Augustus and Regulus
Augustus.note: Horace juxtaposes Augustus's prospective divinity and eastern policy with Regulus's example.

Bagradas serpent.note: Regulus and his army battle an enormous serpent using artillery.
Regulus's army kills the serpent with siege engines and sends its remains to Rome.

Brutus.note: Medieval British genealogy makes Brutus a descendant of Aeneas.

Butes.note: Camilla spears Butes from behind between helmet and breastplate.

Cacus.note: Evander’s community benefits from Cacus’s death, which Evander narrates to Aeneas.

Capys.note: Capys is Aeneas's grandfather in the Assaracid genealogy.

Catillus.note: Catillus is associated with Evander’s expedition in later Tibur traditions.

Celaeno.note: Celaeno prophesies hunger and the Trojans' eating of their tables.

Chloreus.note: Camilla pursues Chloreus for his conspicuous equipment, leaving herself exposed to Arruns.

Christ.myth: Sibylline prophecy reinterpreted as Christian testimony
Christ.note: Christian writers retrospectively present Sibylline and Cumaean material as pagan testimony to Christ.

Chromis.note: Camilla kills Chromis in rapid succession with other warriors.

Chthonian gods.note: Curtius offers himself as Rome's permanent herald and envoy below.

Creusa.note: Creusa is Aeneas's Trojan wife and normally Ascanius's mother.
Her ghost reveals Aeneas's western destiny after she vanishes at Troy.
Virgil makes the Trojan princess Creusa Ascanius’s mother.
Creusa places Ascanius in Aeneas’s care before disappearing during the escape.

Dardanus.note: Aeneas belongs to the Dardanian royal line descending from Dardanus.

Deiphobus.note: Deiphobus's mutilated shade tells Aeneas how Troy fell.
The Sibyl interrupts Aeneas and Deiphobus because their allotted time is passing.

Demophoon.note: Camilla kills Demophoon in rapid succession with other warriors.

Dido.note: Aeneas becomes Dido's lover under divine manipulation before leaving Carthage.
Dido regards Aeneas's secret preparations and departure as betrayal.
Dido silently rejects Aeneas's explanation and returns to Sychaeus.
Dido sends Ascanius gifts and a horse that he later rides.
The Sibyl accompanies Aeneas during his encounter with Dido but does not address her.
Two garments Dido made for Aeneas are placed over Pallas’s corpse.

Diores.note: Diores competes with the pair and benefits from Salius’ fall.

Dira.note: The Dira assumes bird form and terrifies Turnus, announcing his imminent death.

Dyna.note: Marginal mythographic genealogy names Dyna as Evander’s daughter.

Echemus.note: A late human genealogy names Echemus, king of Tegea, as Evander’s father.

Erichthonius.note: Erichthonius is an ancestor in Aeneas's Dardanian genealogy.

Erulus.note: Evander kills the three-lived Erulus three times in combat.

Eryx.note: Aeneas holds Anchises's funeral games in the deceased hero's region.

Eunaeus.note: Camilla kills Eunaeus with a spear through his exposed chest.

Eurydice.note: Late mythographic tradition gives Eurydice as an alternative Trojan wife.
The lost Cypria possibly made Eurydice Ascanius’s mother through her marriage to Aeneas.

Fadus.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Fadus.note: Euryalus kills Fadus during the night raid.

Halaesus.note: After praying to Tiber, Pallas strikes and kills Halaesus.

Harpalycus.note: Camilla kills the male warrior Harpalycus.

Helenus.note: Helenus hosts Aeneas and gives prophetic instructions for his voyage.
Helenus hosts the Trojans and provides farewell gifts while Ascanius is present.

Helymus.note: Helymus competes with the pair and passes Salius after his fall.

Herbesus.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Herbesus.note: Euryalus kills Herbesus during the night raid.

Hercules.note: Aeneas participates in Evander's commemorative rite for Hercules.
Hercules hears Pallas’s prayer and grieves, but Jupiter prevents him from intervening against Turnus.

Hersilia.note: Hersilia is usually Romulus’ Sabine wife and later joins him as Hora.
The deified Romulus receives Hersilia in heaven and renames her Hora.

Hisbo.note: Pallas kills the attacking Hisbo with a sword thrust into his lung.

Horatia.note: She is the sister of the Horatii and mourns her Curiatius fiancé.
She is betrothed to one of the Curiatii.
The surviving Horatius stabs her for mourning her slain Curiatius fiancé.

Horatius the father.note: He is the father of the Horatii and defends the survivor.
He defends his son before the people and helps secure acquittal.
He conducts his son's expiation and leads him beneath the beam.

Hydra of Lerna.note: The African serpent is compared to the Hydra as a literary monster type.

Hyrtacus.note: Nisus is explicitly identified by the patronymic Hyrtacides.

Ilus.note: Pallas casts at Ilus, but the fleeing Rhoeteus intercepts the missile.

Iris.note: Iris incites the Trojan women to burn Aeneas's ships for Juno.
Iris guides Hersilia to Romulus after his transformation into Quirinus.

Iris.myth: Command to attack the Trojan camp
Iris.note: Iris delivers Juno’s instruction that Turnus attack the Trojan camp during Aeneas’s absence.

Janus Curiatius.note: Purificatory sacrifice is offered at his paired altar.

Juno Sororia.note: Purificatory sacrifice is offered at her altar after the sister's killing.

Jupiter Indiges.note: Roman tradition identifies the vanished or deified Aeneas with the local Indiges.

Jupiter Stator.note: A damaged tradition may locate Tarpeia's image or memorial near his temple.

Juturna.note: Juturna guides Turnus toward Pallas, though she never exchanges words with him.
The divine nymph Juturna is identified as Turnus’s sister.
Juturna drives Turnus’s chariot, restores his sword, and delays his encounter with Aeneas.

Lagus.note: Pallas spears Lagus while he is lifting a heavy rock.

Lamus.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Lamus.note: Nisus kills Lamus while he sleeps.

Lamyrus.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Lamyrus.note: Nisus kills Lamyrus while he sleeps.

Larides.note: Pallas cuts off Larides’s right hand during combat.

Larina.note: Larina fights as a maiden warrior in Camilla's company.

Latinus.note: Latinus receives Aeneas, promises Lavinia, and becomes his ally and father-in-law.
One Livian variant has Latinus fight Aeneas before making peace.

Latinus.myth: War caused by the stag’s death
Latinus.note: Ascanius’s manipulated hunting shot destabilizes Latinus’s political order and helps ignite war.

Lausus.note: Aeneas kills Lausus as he protects Mezentius, then immediately pities him.
The opposing youths advance against one another, but Jupiter prevents their duel.

Lavinia, Evander’s daughter.note: Lavinia is Evander’s daughter and Hercules’ partner in Polybius’s genealogy.

Leto.note: Leto heals the wounded Aeneas together with Artemis.

Liris.myth: Paired fall of Liris and Pagasus
Liris.note: Camilla kills Liris during his paired fall with Pagasus.

Lyros.note: Apollodoran mythography makes Lyros another son of Anchises and Aphrodite.

Messapus.myth: Euryalus takes the fatal crested helmet
Messapus.note: Euryalus steals and wears Messapus’ helmet, whose reflection exposes him.

Metabus.note: Metabus is Camilla's father and raises her in exile.

Mezentius.note: Aeneas fights and wounds the Etruscan enemy Mezentius.
Aeneas kills Mezentius after the death of Lausus.
In annalistic variants Ascanius continues the Latin struggle against Mezentius.
Evander explains Mezentius’s cruelty and the Etruscan revolt to Aeneas.

Misenus.note: Misenus is Aeneas's companion, whose burial permits the underworld journey.
The Sibyl reveals Misenus’ unburied corpse and requires his funeral rites.

Mnestheus.myth: Council in the besieged Trojan camp
Mnestheus.note: Mnestheus shares the command and council setting with the pair.

Neptune Equester.myth: Games and abduction of the women
Neptune Equester.note: Plutarch identifies the festival’s honored deity with Neptune Equester.

Neptune Equestris.note: Evander’s Arcadians establish his precinct and equestrian festival.

Numanus Remulus.note: Ascanius answers Numanus’s taunts by killing him with an arrow.

Numicus.note: The river washes away Aeneas's mortal portion before his deification.

Opheltes.note: Euryalus is the son of Opheltes, who raised him amid war.

Opis.note: Opis watches over Camilla and kills Arruns to avenge her death.

Ornytus.note: Camilla kills and taunts the Etruscan hunter-warrior Ornytus.

Orsilochus.note: Camilla outmaneuvers Orsilochus by suddenly reversing her flight.
Camilla kills the pleading Orsilochus with repeated axe blows.

Pagasus.myth: Paired fall of Liris and Pagasus
Pagasus.note: Camilla kills Pagasus during his paired fall with Liris.

Pales.myth: Temple vow after victory over the Sallentini
Pales.note: Regulus allegedly vowed or dedicated a temple to Pales after victory.

Palinurus.note: Palinurus serves as Aeneas's helmsman until he is lost at sea.
Aeneas encounters the unburied shade of his lost helmsman.
The Sibyl refuses his unlawful crossing but foretells burial and a place named for him.

Pallantia.note: Late commentary names Pallantia as Evander’s daughter and possible eponym.

Pallas, Arcadian ancestor.note: An ancestral Pallas is the forebear and eponym of Evander’s Arcadian people.

Pallas, son of Hercules and Lavinia.note: Pallas is Evander’s grandson through Lavinia and Hercules.
Evander raises Pallas’s tomb and names Pallantium for him.

Pan Lycaeus.note: Evander’s Arcadians establish or transfer Pan’s cult to the Lupercal.

Pandarus.note: Pandarus fights beside Aeneas from his chariot before Diomedes kills him.

Panopes.note: Panopes competes against Nisus and Euryalus in the footrace.

Patron.note: Patron accompanies Evander during his migration and settlement.
Patron competes against Nisus and Euryalus in the footrace.

Pilumnus.note: Turnus descends from Pilumnus, an Italian divine or ancestral figure.

Polydorus.note: The murdered Trojan's bleeding grave warns Aeneas to leave Thrace.

Priam, son of Polites.note: Priam leads one mounted squadron alongside Ascanius in the Trojan youth display.

Rhamnes.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Rhamnes.note: Nisus kills Turnus’ sleeping kingly augur.
Euryalus takes Rhamnes’ phalerae and golden-studded belt.

Rhoeteus.note: Pallas kills fleeing Rhoeteus with a missile originally aimed at Ilus.

Rhoetus.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Rhoetus.note: Euryalus kills Rhoetus as he rises from hiding behind a bowl.

Rome.note: Some late genealogical material assigns Rome as Evander’s daughter.

Rumina.note: Antiquarians associate the nursing goddess with the twins’ suckling and sacred fig.

Sabine.note: Corneille invents Sabine as the Alban wife of the Roman Horace.
Corneille's Sabine is an Alban woman related to the Curiatii.

Salius.note: Salius competes against Nisus and Euryalus in the footrace.

Salius.myth: Nisus obstructs Salius during the footrace
Salius.note: Nisus deliberately trips Salius so that Euryalus can win.

Serestus.myth: Council in the besieged Trojan camp
Serestus.note: Serestus shares the command and council setting with the pair.

Serranus.myth: Massacre in the sleeping Rutulian camp
Serranus.note: Nisus kills the handsome young Serranus after his drinking and gaming.

Silvia.note: Ascanius unknowingly kills Silvia’s domesticated stag, and her lament summons the country people.

Silvius.note: Virgil makes Silvius the son of Aeneas and Lavinia.
Alternative annalistic genealogies make Silvius Aeneas's later descendant through Ascanius.
Livy and Ovid make Silvius the son and successor of Ascanius.
Dionysius makes Silvius Ascanius’s younger half-brother through Aeneas and Lavinia.

Sol Indiges.note: Later antiquarian interpretation uncertainly connects Aeneas Indiges with Lavinium's solar divinity.

Spurius Larcius.note: Larcius fights beside Cocles, then withdraws on his order.

Spurius Tarpeius.note: Tarpeia is the daughter of the Roman commander of the citadel.

Sthenius.note: Pallas directly attacks Sthenius during his battlefield advance.

Sulmo.note: Nisus kills Sulmo with his first missile from concealment.

Tagus.note: Nisus kills Tagus with his second missile.

Tarchon.note: Evander directs Aeneas toward Tarchon’s forces, which require a foreign commander.

Tereus.note: Camilla kills Tereus in rapid succession with other warriors.

The immortal gods.note: Curtius looks toward their temples and raises his hands heavenward.
They allegedly permit Carthaginian cruelty so Regulus earns greater glory.

Thymber.note: Pallas severs the head of Thymber, twin brother of Larides.

Tiber.note: Pallas prays for aid against Halaesus, vows spoils, and the river-god hears.
The flooded river receives the exposed twins and deposits them near the Palatine.

Tiberinus.note: The river god appears in a dream and guides Aeneas to Evander.

Tiberinus.myth: Prayer before the leap into the Tiber
Tiberinus.note: Cocles asks the river-god to receive his weapons and warrior favorably.

Timandra.note: A late human genealogy names Timandra as Evander’s mother.

Titus Herminius.note: Herminius fights beside Cocles, then withdraws on his order.

Titus Tatius.note: Antigonus alternatively makes Tarpeia Tatius's captive daughter acting for him.

Titus Tatius.myth: The bargain for what the Sabines wore
Titus Tatius.note: Seeking gold ornaments, Tarpeia receives the Sabines' crushing shields instead.

Titus Tatius.myth: Tarpeia's attempted disarming of the Sabines
Titus Tatius.note: Tarpeia requests Sabine shields intending to disarm Tatius's forces.
Tatius begins Tarpeia's execution by ordering or casting shields upon her.
Tarpeia loves Tatius, imagines marriage, and offers the citadel as dowry.

Tros.note: Tros is an ancestor in Aeneas's Dardanian genealogy.

Tulla.note: Tulla fights as a maiden warrior in Camilla's company.

Tyrrhus.note: Tyrrhus joins the armed rural response after Ascanius kills his household’s stag.

Unnamed son of Aunus.note: The Ligurian tricks Camilla into dismounting by proposing a foot fight.
Camilla exposes his trick, overtakes him, and kills him.

Venilia.note: Venilia, a sea-associated nymph or marine divinity, is Turnus’s mother.

Venus Cloacina.note: Modern scholars conjecture that the statue called Cloelia originally represented Venus Cloacina.

Venus Equestris.note: Modern scholars conjecture that the statue called Cloelia originally represented Venus Equestris.

Vica Pota.note: Modern scholars conjecture that the statue called Cloelia originally represented Vica Pota.

Victory.note: Evander’s Arcadians establish Victory’s Palatine precinct and sacrifices.

Volcens.note: Volcens kills Euryalus despite Nisus claiming sole responsibility.
Nisus drives his sword into Volcens’ mouth before dying.

the Naiads.note: Following Tarpeia's betrayal, the Naiads create heated water obstructing the Sabines.

the Sun.note: The champions look toward the Sun before beginning the combat.

the common family gods.note: Both related groups invoke their shared ancestral gods before fighting.
